_notes: Coordinates are working centroids; Imja Tsho was corrected to 27.898N 86.928E (the old value was Everest's summit). Lumding and Hongu coordinates and altitudes are still UNVERIFIED: run pipeline/gee_landsat.py --verify-positions. lakes.name: Imja Tsho
lakes.context: Formed at the foot of the Imja and Lhotse Shar glaciers from the 1950s, and described in a 2009 study as one of the fastest-growing glacial lakes in the Himalaya. A 2016 outlet project drained over 4 million cubic metres.
lakes.key_stat: About 0.84 km² in 2000 to 1.27 km² in 2015 (Rounce et al. 2016).

exposure.places_note: Villages along the Imja Khola and Dudh Koshi trail corridor.
exposure.mitigation: In 2016 outlet works drained over 4 million cubic metres from the lake (UNDP and Government of Nepal).
exposure.note: Public geography and infrastructure only, from the sources listed in the fact sheet. No flood travel times, populations or discharges are modelled on this site.

lakes.name: Tsho Rolpa
lakes.context: One of the largest glacial lakes in Nepal, fed by the Trakarding Glacier. Its level was lowered 3 m by 2000. About 6,000 households lie downstream.
lakes.key_stat: Close to steady at 1.5 to 1.6 km² since 2000 (Rounce et al. 2016; ICIMOD 2019).

exposure.places_note: Rolwaling valley villages, down to the Tama Koshi.
infrastructure: Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower (456 MW), on the Tama Koshi river system the Rolwaling valley drains into
exposure.mitigation: The lake level was lowered 3 m by 2000 with an outlet channel (ICIMOD).
exposure.note: Public geography and infrastructure only, from the sources listed in the fact sheet. No flood travel times, populations or discharges are modelled on this site.

lakes.name: Thulagi (Dona)
lakes.context: Dona Tal sits southwest of Manaslu at about 4,044 m. Two hydropower projects, Marsyangdi and Middle Marsyangdi, are downstream. ICIMOD surveyed it in the field in 2011.
lakes.key_stat: 0.76 km² in 1995 to 0.94 km² in 2009, about 0.95 km² since (ICIMOD 2011; Rounce et al. 2016).

places: Marsyangdi valley, Manang and Lamjung districts
exposure.places_note: The lake drains into the Marsyangdi river.
exposure.mitigation: No mitigation work recorded in the sources we used.
exposure.note: Public geography and infrastructure only, from the sources listed in the fact sheet. No flood travel times, populations or discharges are modelled on this site.

lakes.name: Lower Barun
lakes.context: Formed by the retreating West Barun Glacier in Makalu Barun National Park, near the Makalu base camp trail. It grew by about three quarters between 2000 and 2015.
lakes.key_stat: 0.95 km² in 2000 to 1.67 km² in 2015, about +76% (Rounce et al. 2016). The fastest-growing lake in this set.

places: Barun and Arun valleys, Sankhuwasabha district
exposure.places_note: Downstream settlements and infrastructure are not yet mapped by us.
exposure.mitigation: No mitigation work recorded in the sources we used.

lakes.name: Lumding Tsho
lakes.context: A moraine-dammed lake in eastern Nepal whose glacier reaches the water. Rounce et al. (2016) rate its hazard High.
lakes.key_stat: 0.77 km² in 2000 to 1.12 km² in 2015, about +44% (Rounce et al. 2016).

lakes.name: Hongu (Chamlang South)
lakes.context: Chamlang South Tsho, below the south face of Chamlang. Stable in size, but Rounce et al. (2016) rate its hazard Very High because of steep glacier and moraine conditions.
lakes.key_stat: About 0.82 km² and steady from 2000 to 2015 (Rounce et al. 2016).
